questions.stem: Far from being the (i)_____ figure of popular legend, toiling alone in his laboratory and indifferent to rivals, the chemist kept up an enormous correspondence and was (ii)_____ about questions of priority, rushing results into print whenever a competitor seemed close.
questions.explain: Clues: 'far from' reverses the legend, and the legend is glossed right after the blank: 'toiling alone ... indifferent to rivals'. So blank (i) predicts 'solitary': reclusive. Blank (ii) must reverse 'indifferent to rivals' and match 'rushing results into print': watchful, anxious. Vigilant fits. Trap: nonchalant matches the legend, not the reality; it is the opposite-direction word. Convivial is the reverse of what the legend says, so it cannot describe the legend. Magnanimous (generous toward rivals) clashes with racing them into print. reclusive = withdrawn from society; convivial = sociable, festive; nonchalant = casually unconcerned; magnanimous = generous, forgiving. Lesson: after 'far from X', the sentence defines X by the very words it later reverses; fill X with the legend, not the truth.

questions.stem: The drug's side effects, though rarely dangerous, were so (i)_____ (nausea, insomnia, and a persistent metallic taste) that many patients abandoned the regimen within weeks. Its disappointing results in practice were thus (ii)_____ poor adherence rather than any pharmacological shortcoming.
questions.explain: Clues: 'though rarely dangerous' sets up a contrast, and 'so ... that many patients abandoned' is consequence: the effects must be burdensome enough to make people quit. Predict 'unbearable': onerous. Trap: innocuous echoes 'rarely dangerous' locally, but harmless effects would not drive patients away, and 'though' demands a contrast with harmlessness. Idiosyncratic (peculiar to individuals) gives no reason for mass abandonment. Blank (ii): 'thus' plus 'rather than any pharmacological shortcoming' says the cause of failure was adherence: attributable to. Unrelated to reverses the logic; disguised by implies a hidden success. onerous = burdensome; innocuous = harmless; idiosyncratic = peculiar to one person. Lesson: in a 'so X that Y' sentence, X must be strong enough to cause Y; a word that only echoes a nearby concession fails.

questions.stem: The planet's placid, banded appearance in amateur telescopes belies the (i)_____ of its atmosphere, where storms larger than Earth persist for centuries. Astronomers who once regarded the bands as (ii)_____ features now understand them as the visible traces of violent, ever-shifting jet streams.
questions.explain: Clues: 'belies' means the appearance gives a false impression, so the reality is the opposite of 'placid': predict 'violence'. Turbulence fits, confirmed by 'storms larger than Earth'. Trap: tranquility repeats the false appearance, the classic belies error. Blank (ii): 'once regarded ... now understand' is a reversal; now they are 'ever-shifting', so once they seemed unchanging: static. Trap: ephemeral (short-lived) sounds like 'shifting', but that is the current view, not the discarded one. Luminous has no link to the contrast. belies = gives a false picture of; ephemeral = lasting a very short time; static = unchanging. Lesson: 'once thought X, now known Y' means X is the opposite of Y; do not fill X with Y's synonym.

questions.stem: Because the strata had been folded and overturned by later tectonic activity, the oldest rocks now lay atop the youngest. Hence the usual principle that deeper layers are older was, at this site, a (i)_____ guide, and geologists had to rely on fossil assemblages to establish a (ii)_____ chronology.
questions.explain: Clues: the rocks are upside down, and 'hence' draws the consequence: a rule that says 'deeper is older' would give the wrong order. Predict 'deceptive': misleading. Trap: reliable is the opposite. Redundant (unneeded) is wrong because the rule was not merely superfluous; it pointed the wrong way, which is why other evidence was required. Blank (ii): geologists turned to fossils to get a correct sequence, so predict 'trustworthy': sound. Trap: inverted sounds related to 'overturned', but an inverted chronology is what the faulty rule would produce, not what the fossils fixed. Spurious (false) contradicts the purpose. redundant = superfluous; spurious = false, not genuine. Lesson: follow 'hence' as a chain: overturned rocks, rule fails, other evidence gives the true answer.

questions.stem: Although the invasive mussel was at first welcomed for clearing the lake's murky water, its effects proved far from (i)_____: by filtering out the plankton on which native fish larvae fed, it (ii)_____ the very food web whose recovery the clearer water had seemed to signal.
questions.explain: Clues: 'although ... welcomed' signals that the effects turned out bad, and 'far from X' means X is the good thing it was not. Predict 'harmless': benign. Trap: deleterious (harmful) is the reality, but 'far from deleterious' would mean harmless, the reverse of the sentence. Conspicuous is irrelevant. Blank (ii): removing the larvae's food damages the food web, and 'whose recovery ... had seemed to signal' marks irony: it got worse. Predict 'depleted': impoverished. Enriched and stabilized repeat the false appearance. benign = harmless, gentle; deleterious = harmful. Lesson: 'far from X' wants X to be the opposite of the truth; if you pick the truth word, you have flipped the sentence.

questions.stem: Wegener's hypothesis of drifting continents met with such (i)_____ from the geological establishment that for decades few researchers dared to cite it approvingly; only when mapping of the seafloor revealed spreading ridges was the idea (ii)_____, and its author honored posthumously.
questions.explain: Clues: 'such X ... that few dared to cite it approvingly' is consequence: X must make support risky. Predict 'contempt': scorn. Trap: acclaim is the opposite; curiosity would invite citation, not deter it. Blank (ii): 'only when' new evidence appeared, and 'honored posthumously', so the idea was proved right: vindicated. Trap: repudiated (rejected) is the opposite and clashes with 'honored'. Broached (first raised) is wrong because the idea had been proposed decades earlier. vindicated = shown to be right; repudiated = rejected, disowned; broached = raised for discussion. Lesson: a 'such X that Y' clause lets you derive X from its effect Y; read the effect first.

questions.stem: The physician's notes were notoriously (i)_____, often a single cryptic line per visit, so that colleagues inheriting his patients had to (ii)_____ treatment histories from pharmacy records and the patients' own recollections.
questions.explain: Clues: 'a single cryptic line per visit' defines blank (i): very brief. Predict 'terse': laconic. Trap: prolix (wordy) is the paired opposite he tends to confuse with it. Meticulous (careful, detailed) contradicts 'cryptic'. Blank (ii): 'so that' gives the consequence of thin notes: colleagues had to rebuild the histories from other sources. Reconstruct. Trap: corroborate means confirm something you already have; here there was nothing to confirm. Disregard reverses the effort described. laconic = using very few words; prolix = tediously long-winded; meticulous = extremely careful; corroborate = confirm with evidence. Lesson: when a pair like laconic/prolix appears, tie the word to a concrete clue (one line per visit) rather than to a vague sense of 'writing style'.

questions.stem: The so-called supermoon is not merely an illusion: it occurs when a full moon coincides with (i)_____, the point in its orbit at which the Moon is closest to Earth, so that its disk appears measurably larger. Yet the difference, roughly fourteen percent in diameter, is (ii)_____ enough that most casual observers would not notice it without a side-by-side comparison.
questions.explain: Clues: blank (i) is defined in the sentence: 'the point ... closest to Earth'. That is perigee. Trap: apogee is the farthest point, the paired opposite. Zenith (the point directly overhead in the sky) sounds astronomical but is not an orbital distance. Blank (ii): 'Yet' turns from 'measurably larger', and 'would not notice' is the result of 'so ... enough that'. Predict 'small': modest. Trap: palpable (easily perceived) contradicts 'would not notice'. Egregious (outstandingly bad) is off-target. perigee = orbital point nearest Earth; apogee = farthest point, also a peak; zenith = highest point overhead; palpable = obvious, tangible. Lesson: anchor peri- (near, around) and apo- (away from); in a 'X enough that Y' clause, X must cause Y.

questions.stem: The volcano had been dormant for so long that local residents regarded it as (i)_____, a scenic backdrop rather than a hazard; the seismologists' warnings of renewed activity were thus dismissed as (ii)_____, even as the ground on its flanks began to swell.
questions.explain: Clues: 'so long that' plus 'a scenic backdrop rather than a hazard' says residents saw it as lifeless. Predict 'harmless, inactive': inert. Trap: menacing and capricious (unpredictable) describe a hazard, the opposite of their view. Blank (ii): 'thus' gives the consequence of complacency, and 'dismissed as' needs a dismissive label: needlessly frightening, alarmist. Trap: prescient (foreseeing correctly) is what the warnings actually were, as 'even as the ground began to swell' implies, but nobody dismisses a warning by calling it prescient. Perfunctory (done carelessly) is not the residents' complaint. inert = inactive, motionless; capricious = given to sudden changes; prescient = having foresight; perfunctory = done as a routine, without care. Lesson: 'dismissed as' takes the speaker's view, not the author's; do not fill in the truth.

questions.stem: The desert's apparent barrenness belies its (i)_____: a single heavy rain can trigger the germination of seeds that have lain dormant for decades, carpeting the ground with flowers within days. Such (ii)_____ seeds, able to wait out years of drought, are the key to the ecosystem's persistence.
questions.explain: Clues: 'belies' means the appearance (barrenness) is false, so the truth is the opposite: fertility. Fecundity fits, confirmed by 'carpeting the ground with flowers'. Trap: sterility and aridity repeat the false appearance. Blank (ii): seeds that 'wait out years of drought' are tough and durable: hardy. Trap: ephemeral (short-lived) describes the flowers, not the seeds that last decades. Fragile contradicts 'wait out years of drought'. fecundity = fertility, productiveness; ephemeral = lasting a short time; hardy = able to endure difficult conditions. Lesson: with 'belies', the blank is the hidden reality, the opposite of the surface; check that the next sentence describes the same thing you chose.

questions.stem: Far from embracing Semmelweis's evidence that handwashing reduced deaths from childbed fever, many of his colleagues found it (i)_____, since it implied that physicians themselves were carrying the disease from patient to patient. Their resistance, then, was less a matter of scientific doubt than of professional (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: 'far from embracing' and 'since it implied that physicians themselves were carrying the disease' says the evidence offended them. Predict 'insulting, irritating': galling. Trap: persuasive is what 'far from embracing' rules out. Abstruse (hard to understand) is excluded by 'less a matter of scientific doubt'. Blank (ii): resistance rooted in wounded self-image is pride: vanity. Trap: humility is the opposite; a humble profession would accept blame. Rigor names a scientific virtue, but the sentence says the motive was not scientific. galling = irritating, humiliating; abstruse = obscure, hard to grasp; vanity = excessive pride in oneself. Lesson: 'less X than Y' sets X and Y apart; if X is 'scientific doubt', Y cannot be a scientific virtue.

questions.stem: Early telescopic views of Mars were so (i)_____ by atmospheric blurring that chance alignments of faint dark patches were taken for straight channels. The famous 'canals' were thus less a discovery than an (ii)_____, born of the observers' eagerness to see order where there was none.
questions.explain: Clues: 'so X by atmospheric blurring that' patches were misread: blurring must have degraded the views. Predict 'impaired': compromised. Trap: enhanced reverses the effect of blurring. Corroborated (confirmed) makes no sense with 'by blurring'. Blank (ii): 'less a discovery than' sets up the opposite of a real finding, and 'eagerness to see order where there was none' says it was not there: illusion. Trap: anomaly (an irregularity) implies something real but unusual, still a kind of discovery. Axiom (a self-evident principle) does not fit an observation. compromised = weakened, impaired; corroborated = confirmed; anomaly = deviation from the norm; axiom = accepted principle. Lesson: 'less A than B' requires B to stand against A; an anomaly is still a discovery.

questions.stem: The naturalist never claimed that his survey of the region's beetles was exhaustive; his monograph is (i)_____ rather than comprehensive, treating a few representative species in depth. Its lasting value lies in the (ii)_____ of its observations, each recorded with a precision that later specialists have rarely matched.
questions.explain: Clues: 'never claimed ... exhaustive' and 'rather than comprehensive' tell you blank (i) means limited in scope, and 'a few representative species in depth' confirms: selective. Trap: encyclopedic (all-covering) contradicts 'rather than comprehensive', the exact error of choosing 'comprehensive' when the text denies thoroughness of coverage. Superficial fits 'not exhaustive' locally but contradicts 'in depth' and 'precision'. Blank (ii): 'recorded with a precision' defines it: exactitude. Trap: breadth is what the work disclaimed. Novelty is never mentioned. encyclopedic = covering every subject; exactitude = precision, accuracy. Lesson: test blank (i) against every later clause; a word can match the nearest clause and still contradict the rest.

questions.stem: Wolves, by keeping elk on the move, prevent them from overgrazing streamside willows; the predators' reintroduction hence had (i)_____ effects reaching well beyond their direct prey, as recovering willows stabilized stream banks and sheltered songbirds. Ecologists cite the case to rebut the notion that top predators are ecologically (ii)_____, mere passengers on systems they do not shape.
questions.explain: Clues: 'hence' plus 'reaching well beyond their direct prey' and the chain willows, banks, songbirds describes effects spreading step by step: cascading. Trap: negligible contradicts 'well beyond'. Deleterious (harmful) clashes with the recoveries listed. Blank (ii): the notion being rebutted is glossed as 'mere passengers on systems they do not shape': unneeded, inessential. Superfluous fits. Trap: pivotal is what the case proves, the author's view, not the rebutted notion. Rapacious (greedy, predatory) describes behavior, not ecological importance. cascading = spreading in successive stages; deleterious = harmful; superfluous = unnecessary; rapacious = aggressively greedy. Lesson: a blank inside a view being rebutted takes the opponent's position; the appositive after the comma tells you what it is.

questions.stem: Hutton's claim that slow processes still visible today (erosion, sedimentation, uplift) could account for the planet's features required an almost unimaginably (i)_____ timescale. His critics, committed to a young Earth, found the proposal not merely improbable but (ii)_____, an affront to scriptural chronology.
questions.explain: Clues: if slow processes made everything, they needed enormous time, and 'critics committed to a young Earth' objected. Predict 'long': protracted. Trap: truncated (shortened) is the young-Earth view. Uniform sounds related to uniformitarianism, but 'unimaginably uniform timescale' says nothing about length, which is what the logic requires. Blank (ii): 'not merely improbable but X' escalates, and 'an affront to scriptural chronology' defines X as religiously offensive: impious. Trap: plausible reverses 'improbable' instead of intensifying it. Pedantic (fussily academic) misses the religious clue. protracted = prolonged; truncated = cut short; impious = lacking reverence; pedantic = overly concerned with minor details. Lesson: 'not merely X but Y' needs Y stronger in the same direction as X, often glossed by what follows.

questions.stem: Although the new screening test is highly sensitive, catching nearly every true case, it is far less (i)_____, flagging many healthy patients as well. A positive result is therefore best treated as (ii)_____, prompting further examination rather than settling the diagnosis.
questions.explain: Clues: 'although ... catches nearly every case' then 'far less X, flagging many healthy patients': X is the ability to tell sick from healthy. Predict 'able to distinguish': discriminating. Trap: inclusive is what the test is (it includes too many), so 'far less inclusive' reverses the clue. Accessible (easy to obtain) is unrelated to false alarms. Blank (ii): 'therefore' plus 'prompting further examination rather than settling the diagnosis' says the result is tentative: provisional. Trap: conclusive is the opposite. Spurious (false) goes too far: many positives are real, so they need checking, not dismissal. discriminating = able to make fine distinctions; provisional = tentative, pending confirmation; spurious = false, fake. Lesson: when a 'rather than' clause follows, it defines your blank by contrast.

questions.stem: Ptolemy's model, burdened with epicycles upon epicycles, was cumbersome but by no means (i)_____: it predicted planetary positions well enough to serve astronomers and navigators for over a millennium. Copernicus's heliocentric system, for all its conceptual elegance, was at first no more (ii)_____ in its predictions.
questions.explain: Clues: 'cumbersome but by no means X' followed by 'predicted ... well enough to serve ... for over a millennium': X is the opposite of useful. Predict 'useless': ineffectual. Trap: elegant feels like the opposite of cumbersome, but 'but' signals a turn toward a merit, and the colon explains that merit as usefulness. Intricate contradicts 'epicycles upon epicycles'. Blank (ii): 'for all its elegance' concedes a merit, so the blank names a merit it lacked in prediction: precise. Trap: heterodox (unorthodox) is true of Copernicus historically, but 'no more heterodox in its predictions' is meaningless. Ornate (elaborately decorated) is a style word. ineffectual = not producing results; heterodox = departing from accepted belief. Lesson: 'for all its X' concedes X and introduces a shortcoming on a different dimension.

questions.stem: Coral bleaching is not in itself fatal: stressed corals expel their symbiotic algae but can reacquire them if conditions improve. Marine heat waves, however, now arrive so (i)_____ that reefs lack time to recover between episodes, so that what was once a (ii)_____ setback has become a chronic decline.
questions.explain: Clues: 'lack time to recover between episodes' is the consequence of the blank, so the blank concerns the interval between heat waves: they come often. Frequently. Trap: sporadically (occasionally) would leave plenty of recovery time, the opposite. Belatedly (late) says nothing about spacing. Blank (ii): 'once a X setback has become a chronic decline' contrasts X with chronic, and the first sentence says recovery used to occur: temporary, transient. Trap: permanent and catastrophic describe the present state, not the former one; 'was once ... has become' requires a contrast. transient = passing, short-lived; sporadically = at irregular intervals; chronic = persistent, long-lasting. Lesson: 'what was once X has become Y' makes X and Y opposites; read the endpoint word first.

questions.stem: The apparent modernity of Avicenna's call for carefully controlled tests of remedies belies how (i)_____ his medicine remained in other respects; he still explained illness through an imbalance of the four humors. Historians therefore caution against (ii)_____ readings that cast him as a modern scientist born centuries too early.
questions.explain: Clues: 'belies' says the modern appearance is misleading, and 'still explained illness through ... the four humors' shows his medicine was old-fashioned. Predict 'traditional': conservative. Trap: progressive repeats the misleading appearance. Empirical describes the controlled tests, which is the modern-looking part, not the 'other respects'. Blank (ii): readings that make him 'a modern scientist born centuries too early' wrongly project the present into the past: anachronistic. Trap: contextual is the opposite, the kind of reading historians favor. Skeptical readings would doubt his modernity, which historians endorse rather than caution against. anachronistic = misplaced in time, judging the past by present standards; empirical = based on observation. Lesson: 'caution against X readings that do Y' means X names the error Y; do not pick the remedy.

questions.stem: Diamonds form only under immense pressure deep in the mantle, and at the surface they are, strictly speaking, (i)_____: given enough time, they would revert to graphite. That they endure is owed not to any inherent stability but to the extraordinarily (ii)_____ pace of that conversion.
questions.explain: Clues: the colon explains blank (i): 'given enough time, they would revert'. So at the surface they are not in their stable form: unstable, confirmed by 'not to any inherent stability'. Trap: impervious (unaffected) suits the popular image of diamond's hardness but contradicts reversion. Inert (chemically inactive) also implies permanence. Blank (ii): they 'endure' despite instability, so the conversion must be very slow: sluggish. Trap: rapid would destroy them quickly. Erratic (irregular) does not explain survival. impervious = not affected by; inert = lacking the ability to react. Lesson: a colon after a blank is the definition of the blank; trust it over your general knowledge about the subject.

questions.stem: Far from being an (i)_____ advance, the acceptance of germ theory was halting and piecemeal: some surgeons adopted antiseptic methods while still doubting that microbes existed, and others accepted microbes but (ii)_____ the methods as needless fuss.
questions.explain: Clues: 'far from X' is reversed by 'halting and piecemeal', so X means sudden and complete. Abrupt. Trap: incremental (step by step) agrees with 'piecemeal', so 'far from incremental' contradicts the sentence. Inadvertent (unintentional) has no basis in the text. Blank (ii): 'as needless fuss' shows contempt: disparaged. Trap: embraced reverses 'needless fuss'; codified (formally set down) also implies acceptance. abrupt = sudden; incremental = gradual, in small steps; disparaged = belittled, regarded as worthless; codified = arranged into a formal system. Lesson: 'far from X' then a colon: the text after the colon is the opposite of X; a word synonymous with that text is the trap.

questions.stem: Although the comet's return had been predicted to the day, its appearance proved (i)_____: rather than the brilliant spectacle the press had promised, it was a faint smudge visible only through binoculars, a (ii)_____ that left many casual skywatchers disillusioned.
questions.explain: Clues: 'although predicted to the day' requires a contrast, and the colon explains it: 'rather than the brilliant spectacle ... a faint smudge'. Predict 'disappointing': anticlimactic. Trap: punctual fits 'predicted to the day' locally, but there is no contrast between being predicted and being on time, so 'although' breaks. Spectacular is what the press promised. Blank (ii): an outcome that 'left ... disillusioned' is a letdown: comedown. Trap: vindication is true for the astronomers (the date was right), but the clause is about skywatchers' disappointment. Apotheosis (high point) is the opposite. anticlimactic = disappointingly weak after build-up; apotheosis = culmination, peak; vindication = proof of being right. Lesson: the trap often agrees with the concession clause; the blank belongs to the main clause after 'although'.

questions.stem: The label 'hysteria' was applied so (i)_____ in nineteenth-century medicine, attached to nearly any complaint in women that physicians could not explain, that it eventually lost all diagnostic value. By the mid-twentieth century the word had become little more than a (ii)_____, and it was dropped from official classifications.
questions.explain: Clues: 'attached to nearly any complaint' and 'so ... that it lost all diagnostic value' make blank (i) 'without distinction': indiscriminately. Traps: sparingly and precisely are opposites; precise use would preserve diagnostic value. Blank (ii): a term applied to everything becomes a label covering anything: catch-all. Trap: neologism (a newly coined word) fails, since the term was old. Euphemism (a mild word for a harsh thing) misreads the logic: the problem was vagueness, not politeness. indiscriminately = without careful distinction; neologism = newly coined word; euphemism = a softened substitute expression. Lesson: in consequence chains ('so ... that'), the end state must follow from the cause; overuse produces emptiness, not a new word or a softer one.

questions.stem: The prairie's uniform appearance belies its (i)_____: a single hectare may harbor more than two hundred plant species. Conservationists warn that restoration plantings seeded with only a handful of grasses produce landscapes that are visually convincing but ecologically (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: 'belies' reverses 'uniform appearance', and 'two hundred plant species' gives the reality: great variety. Heterogeneity. Trap: homogeneity repeats the uniform appearance, the standard belies error. Antiquity (great age) is not supported by the species count. Blank (ii): 'visually convincing but ecologically X' sets up a contrast, and 'only a handful of grasses' versus two hundred species shows the plantings lack diversity: impoverished. Traps: authentic and robust would agree with 'convincing', so 'but' would break. heterogeneity = diversity of parts; homogeneity = sameness throughout; impoverished = made poor, depleted. Lesson: 'X but Y' with a positive X needs a negative Y; check that the clue numbers (200 vs a handful) point the same way.

questions.stem: Nineteenth-century catastrophists, who attributed the planet's features to sudden upheavals, were long dismissed by gradualists as (i)_____. Yet the discovery that an asteroid impact ended the age of dinosaurs has (ii)_____ their central intuition, if not their particular explanations.
questions.explain: Clues: 'dismissed as X' needs a dismissive label for people proposing sudden upheavals: unrealistic. Fanciful. Trap: prescient (having foresight) is what the next sentence suggests they were, but no one dismisses a rival by calling him prescient. Sober (measured, realistic) is a compliment. Blank (ii): 'Yet' reverses the dismissal, and an impact is a sudden upheaval, so the intuition has been restored to respect: rehabilitated. 'If not their particular explanations' limits the vindication without cancelling it. Trap: refuted contradicts 'Yet'. Obscured makes no sense after a confirming discovery. fanciful = imaginative but unrealistic; prescient = foreseeing; rehabilitated = restored to good standing. Lesson: 'dismissed as' takes the critic's vocabulary; 'Yet' then signals the author's correction.

questions.stem: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses; prescribing them for a common cold is hence not merely (i)_____ but actively harmful, since each unnecessary course gives resistant strains a chance to (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: 'hence' follows from 'act on bacteria, not viruses': against a cold (viral) they do nothing. 'Not merely X but actively harmful' escalates from X, so X is mildly bad: useless. Futile. Traps: efficacious (effective) and prudent (wise) are positive, so the escalation 'but actively harmful' would make no sense. Blank (ii): the harm is resistance; an unnecessary course kills susceptible bacteria and lets resistant ones multiply: proliferate. Traps: atrophy (waste away) and dissipate (scatter, disappear) reverse the danger. futile = pointless, ineffective; efficacious = producing the intended effect; proliferate = increase rapidly; atrophy = waste away. Lesson: 'not merely X but Y' means X and Y point the same way, Y stronger; a positive X cannot escalate to 'harmful'.

questions.stem: Far from being the (i)_____ void it was once imagined to be, interstellar space is threaded with gas and dust in which new stars are continually forming; it is less an emptiness than a (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: 'far from' plus 'void it was once imagined to be' makes blank (i) the old view: empty, lifeless. Barren. Trap: teeming (full) is the new view, so 'far from teeming' would contradict 'threaded with gas and dust'. Luminous (bright) has no support. Blank (ii): 'less an emptiness than X' contrasts with emptiness, and 'new stars are continually forming' supports a place where things are born: nursery. Trap: wasteland is a synonym for emptiness, so 'less an emptiness than a wasteland' is no contrast. Labyrinth (maze) picks up 'threaded' but ignores star formation, the main point. barren = empty, unproductive; teeming = swarming, full. Lesson: in 'less A than B', B must contrast with A and match the evidence given; a vivid word that matches a stray detail is a trap.

questions.stem: Newton's pronouncements on the cause of gravity are strikingly (i)_____: in one letter he dismisses action at a distance as an absurdity no competent thinker could accept, while in other passages he seems to treat attraction as a real property of matter. Scholars who quote either statement alone thus risk making him appear more (ii)_____ than he was.
questions.explain: Clues: the colon shows two opposed positions, so the pronouncements are ambiguous, open to two readings. Equivocal. Trap: unequivocal is the opposite, tempting because each single statement is firm. Voluminous (lengthy) ignores the contradiction. Blank (ii): quoting one side alone hides the ambiguity, making him look more fixed and certain than he was: doctrinaire. Trap: ambivalent is how he actually was, so 'more ambivalent than he was' reverses the logic. Prolific (productive) is a sounds-related distractor for voluminous. equivocal = ambiguous, uncommitted; doctrinaire = rigidly committed to a doctrine; ambivalent = having mixed feelings. Lesson: 'appear more X than he was' means X is the opposite of the truth just described; always ask what the misquotation distorts.

questions.stem: The island's birds evolved without mammalian predators and so became strikingly (i)_____, approaching people and newly introduced cats without any sign of alarm. This very tameness rendered them (ii)_____ once settlers arrived.
questions.explain: Clues: 'evolved without predators and so became X, approaching ... cats without alarm' defines X as lacking caution. Unwary. Trap: skittish (easily frightened) is the opposite. Gregarious (sociable with their own kind) sounds right because the birds approach people, but it describes flocking behavior, not the absence of fear, which the clue stresses. Blank (ii): 'this very tameness' in the presence of cats and settlers makes them easy to kill: vulnerable. Trap: impervious (unaffected) is the opposite. Conspicuous (easily seen) is not a consequence of tameness. unwary = not cautious; skittish = nervous, jumpy; gregarious = fond of company; impervious = unable to be affected. Lesson: match the specific clue ('without alarm'), not a loosely related behavior; gregarious and unwary are not the same idea.

questions.stem: Although earthquake prediction remains (i)_____, earthquake forecasting does not: seismologists cannot say when a given fault will rupture, but they can estimate with considerable confidence the (ii)_____ of a large quake striking a region over the coming decades.
questions.explain: Clues: 'although prediction remains X, forecasting does not' contrasts the two, and 'cannot say when a given fault will rupture' shows prediction is out of reach. Predict 'unattainable': elusive. Traps: routine and feasible describe what forecasting can do, so they break the contrast. Blank (ii): 'over the coming decades' and 'with considerable confidence' point to an estimate of chance over a period: likelihood. Trap: timing contradicts 'cannot say when'. Aftermath (consequences) is not what a forecast of whether a quake will strike estimates. elusive = hard to achieve or grasp; feasible = possible to do. Lesson: a blank in the second half of a contrast must respect the limit stated in the first half; the trap restates exactly what was ruled out.

questions.stem: The spa town's reputation for (i)_____ air was belied by its own parish registers: deaths from consumption there were higher than in the surrounding countryside. Yet the high mortality was partly a statistical (ii)_____, reflecting who came to the town (the sick, in search of a cure) rather than what the town did to them.
questions.explain: Clues: 'reputation ... belied by its own parish registers' showing high deaths means the reputation was for healthy air. Salubrious. Traps: noxious (harmful) and stagnant describe what the registers seemed to show, not the reputation they contradicted. Blank (ii): the parenthesis is the key: the sick came there, so high mortality reflected selection, not the town's air. A result produced by how the data were gathered rather than by reality is an artifact. Trap: verity (truth) contradicts 'reflecting who came ... rather than what the town did'. Triumph has no footing. salubrious = health-giving; noxious = harmful, poisonous; artifact = a distortion produced by the method; verity = truth. Lesson: read the parenthesis; ETS often hides the decisive clue there.

questions.stem: Galileo's observation that Venus displays a full cycle of phases was impossible to square with a Venus circling Earth inside the Sun's orbit; the finding hence (i)_____ the strict Ptolemaic arrangement, though it remained (ii)_____ Tycho's hybrid model, in which the planets circle the Sun while the Sun circles Earth.
questions.explain: Clues: 'impossible to square with' the Ptolemaic picture, and 'hence': the finding damaged it. Undermined. Trap: buttressed (supported) is the opposite. Anticipated (came before) is a time word that misses the logic. Blank (ii): 'though' signals a limit on the damage: the finding did not rule out every Earth-centered scheme, since in Tycho's model Venus circles the Sun, which produces full phases. Compatible with. Trap: irreconcilable with continues the first clause's direction, so 'though' would be pointless. Subordinate to makes no logical sense. buttressed = reinforced; irreconcilable = impossible to make consistent. Lesson: 'X, though Y' means Y qualifies X; if your choice for Y merely repeats X, the 'though' is wasted.

questions.stem: Far from being (i)_____, the sea otter's appetite for urchins protects kelp forests: where otters vanish, urchin numbers explode and the grazers strip the kelp to bare rock. Fishermen who once regarded the otter as a mere (ii)_____ competing with them for shellfish have come to see it as the forest's guardian.
questions.explain: Clues: 'far from X, the appetite protects' makes X the opposite of protective: destructive. Ruinous. Trap: salutary (beneficial) agrees with 'protects', so 'far from salutary' contradicts. Voracious (ravenous) is likely true of the appetite but is not the opposite of 'protects', so it does not complete the reversal. Blank (ii): 'once regarded ... competing with them' versus 'now ... guardian' requires a negative label: pest. Trap: steward (caretaker) is the new view, synonymous with 'guardian'. Curiosity (an oddity) does not compete for anything. ruinous = disastrous, destructive; salutary = beneficial; voracious = wanting great quantities of food; steward = one who manages or protects. Lesson: after 'far from', pick the antonym of the main verb's idea, not a word that is merely true.

questions.stem: Mendel published his results on pea hybrids in an obscure provincial journal and made little effort to promote them, so that his work remained (i)_____ for more than three decades; when it was at last rediscovered in 1900, it was hailed as (ii)_____, having anticipated a field that did not yet exist when it was written.
questions.explain: Clues: 'obscure journal ... little effort to promote ... so that' gives the consequence: nobody noticed. Neglected, confirmed by 'rediscovered'. Traps: celebrated is the opposite; controversial requires an audience to argue, which the work lacked. Blank (ii): 'having anticipated a field that did not yet exist' defines it: ahead of its time. Prescient. Traps: derivative (unoriginal) is the opposite of anticipating; obsolete (out of date) is tempting because the work was decades old, but the clause says it was ahead, not behind. neglected = ignored; derivative = imitative of others; obsolete = outdated; prescient = foreseeing the future. Lesson: in a 'so that' sentence, derive the blank from the cause; then check that the participle clause ('having anticipated') defines the second blank.

questions.stem: Although the surgeon was famously (i)_____ in the operating theater, completing amputations in under a minute in the years before anesthesia, his private papers reveal a man who was anything but (ii)_____ outside it, agonizing for weeks over whether to operate at all.
questions.explain: Clues: 'completing amputations in under a minute' defines blank (i): swift. Expeditious. Traps: deliberate (slow, careful) and hesitant contradict the speed. Blank (ii): 'anything but X ... agonizing for weeks' means X is the opposite of agonizing: decisive, which also contrasts with his speed in theater as 'although' requires. Trap: irresolute (indecisive) is what he actually was, so 'anything but irresolute' reverses the meaning; it is the opposite-direction word. Meticulous (careful) does not oppose agonizing. expeditious = quick and efficient; deliberate = careful, unhurried; irresolute = unable to decide. Lesson: 'anything but X' is a negation; choose the opposite of the description that follows, then check that 'although' contrasts the two halves.

questions.stem: The (i)_____ look of the rock, a dull gray mudstone indistinguishable from countless others, belies its scientific importance: it preserves in microscopic detail the soft-bodied creatures of a sea that vanished half a billion years ago. Slabs once quarried as (ii)_____ building stone are now guarded in museum vaults.
questions.explain: Clues: 'a dull gray mudstone indistinguishable from countless others' defines blank (i): ordinary. Prosaic. Trap: esoteric (understood by few, specialized) is his paired opposite of prosaic; it matches 'scientific importance' but not the description of how the rock looks. Striking contradicts 'dull'. Blank (ii): 'once quarried as X ... now guarded in museum vaults' contrasts past use with present value, so X is ordinary: workaday. Trap: priceless is the present view. Ornamental (decorative) contradicts 'dull gray'. prosaic = commonplace, unremarkable; esoteric = known only to a small group; workaday = ordinary, everyday. Lesson: with 'belies', the blank sits on the deceptive surface; the clue right after it (dull gray) is the definition.

questions.stem: Light from distant galaxies takes billions of years to reach us, so that a telescope is in effect a time machine: the more remote the object, the more (i)_____ the image it records. Observations of the farthest galaxies are thus not portraits of the universe as it is but (ii)_____ of its infancy.
questions.explain: Clues: 'takes billions of years to reach us, so that' the image is old; 'the more remote, the more X' means older. Archaic. Trap: current is the reverse, because the light left long ago. Luminous is wrong: farther objects look fainter, not brighter. Blank (ii): 'not portraits of the universe as it is but X of its infancy' says the images preserve the past: relics. Trap: forecasts points to the future, the opposite time direction. Caricatures (exaggerated distortions) wrongly implies the images are false rather than old. archaic = belonging to a much earlier period; relics = surviving remnants of the past; caricatures = exaggerated depictions. Lesson: trace the consequence ('so that ... thus') step by step; a time-direction slip is an opposite trap.

questions.stem: Although bats harbor an unusual number of viruses capable of infecting humans, they themselves rarely fall ill, a (i)_____ that researchers attribute to an immune system that tolerates infection rather than fighting it aggressively. Far from making bats (ii)_____ to disease, this restraint may be what keeps them healthy.
questions.explain: Clues: 'although they harbor ... viruses, they rarely fall ill': a seemingly contradictory fact that needs explaining. Paradox. Trap: corollary (a natural consequence) implies the outcome is expected, but 'although' marks it as surprising. Misnomer (a wrongly applied name) needs a name, and none is mentioned. Blank (ii): 'far from making bats X, this restraint may keep them healthy' makes X the opposite of healthy: prone to illness. Susceptible. Trap: immune agrees with 'keeps them healthy', so 'far from immune' contradicts. Indifferent is meaningless here. paradox = a seemingly self-contradictory truth; corollary = a proposition that follows from another; misnomer = a wrong or inaccurate name. Lesson: 'although' tells you the fact is surprising; corollary means unsurprising.

questions.stem: Darwin, keenly aware that his theory would scandalize, was so (i)_____ about publishing it that he spent two decades accumulating evidence; only the arrival of Wallace's strikingly similar essay (ii)_____ him into print.
questions.explain: Clues: 'aware that his theory would scandalize' and 'so X ... that he spent two decades' gathering evidence: X means cautious, reluctant. Chary. Trap: eager is the opposite and clashes with a twenty-year delay. Cavalier (offhand, careless) is also the opposite of caution. Blank (ii): 'only the arrival' of a rival essay finally made him publish, so it pushed him: goaded. Trap: dissuaded (talked out of) reverses the outcome, 'into print'. Absolved (freed from blame) is unrelated. chary = cautious, wary; cavalier = showing arrogant disregard; goaded = provoked or driven to act; dissuaded = persuaded not to. Lesson: 'only X did Y' means X caused the long-awaited action; the blank pushes toward the outcome, not away from it.

questions.stem: Far from being (i)_____, glaciers flow like extraordinarily viscous rivers, their ice deforming under its own weight. Boulders carried hundreds of kilometers from their source rocks testify to this (ii)_____ but relentless motion.
questions.explain: Clues: 'far from X, glaciers flow' makes X the opposite of flowing: motionless. Immobile. Trap: fluid agrees with 'flow', so 'far from fluid' contradicts. Fragile is irrelevant to movement. Blank (ii): 'X but relentless' needs a contrast with relentless, and 'extraordinarily viscous' suggests very slow: imperceptible. Trap: precipitous (steep, very fast) contradicts viscous ice. Erratic is a sounds-related trap: geologists call transported boulders 'erratics', but 'erratic ... but relentless' is a poor contrast and nothing suggests irregular motion. immobile = not moving; precipitous = sudden, steep; erratic = irregular, unpredictable; imperceptible = too slight to be noticed. Lesson: 'X but Y' sets up a contrast; reject a word that only echoes the topic's jargon.

questions.stem: In early trials of the procedure, patients who underwent a sham operation reported as much relief as those who received the real one. The surgery's benefits were hence revealed to be largely (i)_____, and its once-enthusiastic advocates found their testimonials (ii)_____ by the controlled evidence.
questions.explain: Clues: a fake operation worked as well as the real one, so 'hence' the surgery itself contributed little: its benefits were not real effects of the surgery. Illusory. Trap: tangible (real, concrete) is the opposite. Enduring is about duration, which the trial did not test. Blank (ii): 'once-enthusiastic' signals a reversal, and the controlled evidence went against them: their testimonials were weakened. Undercut. Trap: bolstered (supported) is the opposite. Anticipated (came before) is a time word. illusory = based on illusion, not real; tangible = perceptible, concrete; undercut = weakened, undermined; bolstered = supported, strengthened. Lesson: 'once-enthusiastic' is a reversal signal; pick the word that shows the enthusiasm being contradicted.

questions.stem: Although she made the discovery of pulsars as a graduate student, the astronomer was notably (i)_____ about her role, consistently deflecting credit toward her supervisors. Colleagues who expected (ii)_____ from someone so often passed over for honors found instead an unfailing graciousness.
questions.explain: Clues: 'consistently deflecting credit toward her supervisors' defines blank (i): modest, keeping herself in the background. Self-effacing. Trap: vainglorious (boastful) is the opposite. Candid (frank) does not fit deflecting credit. Blank (ii): 'found instead an unfailing graciousness' means the expected trait was its opposite, and being 'passed over for honors' explains the expectation: bitterness. Rancor. Trap: gratitude agrees with graciousness, so 'instead' would make no sense. Diffidence (shyness) echoes self-effacing but is not the opposite of graciousness. self-effacing = modest, avoiding attention; vainglorious = excessively proud; rancor = bitter resentment; diffidence = shyness from lack of confidence. Lesson: 'expected X ... found instead Y' makes X the opposite of Y; then confirm with the stated reason for the expectation.

questions.stem: The tundra's harsh climate belies its (i)_____: the plants that survive there grow so slowly that a single set of tire tracks can remain visible for decades. Land managers have thus learned that an environment hostile to life is not necessarily (ii)_____ disturbance.
questions.explain: Clues: 'belies' says the harsh climate gives a false impression (toughness), and 'tire tracks can remain visible for decades' shows easy, lasting damage: delicacy. Fragility. Trap: resilience matches the false impression of harshness, the classic belies error. Barrenness agrees with the harsh climate, so there is nothing to belie. Blank (ii): 'hostile to life is not necessarily X disturbance' must say a harsh place is not necessarily tough: impervious to. Trap: susceptible to is the reality, so 'not necessarily susceptible' reverses the lesson. Hospitable to makes no sense with disturbance. belies = contradicts, gives a false impression of; impervious = not affected by. Lesson: in 'is not necessarily X', X is the assumption being denied; fill it with the naive belief, not the conclusion.

questions.stem: Historians now regard Newton's alchemical studies not as a (i)_____ from his real science but as continuous with it; far from an embarrassing (ii)_____, they reflect the same experimental patience that produced his work on optics.
questions.explain: Clues: 'not as X ... but as continuous with it' makes X the opposite of continuous: a turning away. Digression. Trap: continuation agrees with 'continuous', so 'not as a continuation but as continuous' is no contrast. Culmination (the peak) also implies continuity. Blank (ii): 'far from an embarrassing X' needs something that would embarrass, and it must contrast with 'the same experimental patience': a departure from his normal character. Aberration. Trap: foundation would not be 'embarrassing'. Triumph contradicts 'embarrassing'. digression = a departure from the main subject; culmination = highest point; aberration = a departure from what is normal. Lesson: 'not as X but as Y' and 'far from X' both demand X opposite to the stated view; test whether the adjective ('embarrassing') fits the noun.

questions.stem: The correlation between coffee drinking and heart disease reported in early studies proved (i)_____: heavy coffee drinkers were also more likely to smoke, so that once smoking was accounted for, the apparent link (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clues: the colon explains blank (i): smoking was the real cause, so the coffee link was false, and 'apparent link' confirms it only seemed real. Spurious. Trap: veracious (truthful) is the opposite, part of his specious/veracious confusion. Robust (strong, holding up) also says the link was real. Blank (ii): 'so that once smoking was accounted for' gives the consequence of removing the confounder: the link disappeared. Evaporated. Traps: intensified and persisted would mean coffee had an effect after all, contradicting 'proved spurious'. spurious = false though seemingly genuine; veracious = truthful, accurate; robust = strong, holding up under scrutiny. Lesson: blank (ii) must agree with blank (i); if the link was spurious, it cannot persist once the true cause is removed.

questions.stem: Because the region's aquifer was filled by rain that fell thousands of years ago and receives almost no recharge today, the water drawn from it is, in effect, (i)_____: once pumped, it is gone. Current rates of pumping are thus less a sustainable harvest than the (ii)_____ of an inheritance that cannot be replaced.
questions.explain: Clues: 'almost no recharge today', 'once pumped, it is gone' and 'cannot be replaced' define blank (i): once used, gone. Nonrenewable. Trap: perennial (lasting, recurring year after year) is the opposite. Abundant may seem true of a large aquifer, but the sentence's logic is about replacement, not quantity. Blank (ii): 'less a sustainable harvest than X' needs the opposite of sustainable use: wasteful use. Squandering. Trap: cultivation means tending something that renews, which the sentence denies. Replenishment (refilling) contradicts 'no recharge'. perennial = lasting or recurring indefinitely; squandering = wasting recklessly. Lesson: 'less A than B' makes B the contrast to A; the clue words (no recharge, cannot be replaced) must hold for both blanks.

questions.stem: The tidy narrative of a lone genius overturning centuries of error belies the (i)_____ character of the Copernican revolution, which unfolded over generations and drew on the work of many hands. Such (ii)_____ accounts flatter our love of heroes at the expense of historical accuracy.
questions.explain: Clues: 'belies' reverses 'lone genius', and 'drew on the work of many hands' gives the reality: shared effort. Collective. Trap: solitary repeats the false narrative. Abrupt contradicts 'unfolded over generations' and also matches the myth, not the reality. Blank (ii): 'such' points back to the 'tidy narrative', and 'at the expense of historical accuracy' says it oversimplifies: simplistic. Trap: nuanced is the opposite. Iconoclastic (attacking cherished beliefs) is a sounds-related trap: the hero in the story is an iconoclast, but the accounts themselves flatter, rather than attack, popular beliefs. collective = shared by a group; iconoclastic = attacking established ideas; nuanced = showing subtle distinctions. Lesson: 'such' refers back; pick a word describing the account, not its hero.

questions.stem: Although the salmon's reproductive strategy seems (i)_____ (each female releases thousands of eggs, nearly all of which perish), it is in fact finely calibrated to rivers in which survival is largely a matter of chance. What looks like waste is a (ii)_____ hedge against unpredictable floods and predators.
questions.explain: Clues: the parenthesis defines blank (i): thousands of eggs, most lost, which the next sentence calls 'what looks like waste'. Predict 'wasteful': prodigal. Trap: parsimonious (stingy) is the opposite. Precarious (insecure, risky) describes the eggs' survival odds, not the strategy's apparent wastefulness. Blank (ii): 'although it seems wasteful, it is in fact finely calibrated': the reality is sensible: prudent. Trap: reckless restates the false appearance. Futile contradicts 'finely calibrated'. prodigal = recklessly wasteful, lavish; parsimonious = extremely frugal; precarious = dangerously unstable; prudent = wise, careful about the future. Lesson: 'seems X ... in fact Y' sets appearance against reality; each blank must sit on the correct side.

questions.stem: The ward physician's examinations, far from being (i)_____, were so thorough that they often uncovered conditions entirely unrelated to the complaint that had brought the patient in. This (ii)_____ endeared him to patients but exasperated administrators who tracked how many cases he saw each day.
questions.explain: Clues: 'far from X, were so thorough' makes X the opposite of thorough: careless, routine. Perfunctory. Trap: exhaustive is a synonym of thorough, so 'far from exhaustive, so thorough' contradicts itself. Intrusive does not oppose thoroughness. Blank (ii): 'this' refers back to the thoroughness, which also slowed his case count: diligent care. Assiduity. Traps: negligence is the opposite. Brusqueness (curt rudeness) would not endear him to patients. perfunctory = done as a routine duty, without care; assiduity = constant, careful attention; brusqueness = abrupt, curt manner. Lesson: 'this X' summarizes what was just described; and 'far from' needs the antonym of the clue, not its synonym.

questions.stem: Because the meteorite had lain in the Antarctic ice for millennia, skeptics argued that its apparent microfossils could be (i)_____, terrestrial microbes that had seeped in after it landed. Its defenders, unable to rule this out, were forced to retreat to the more (ii)_____ claim that the structures were merely consistent with ancient life on Mars.
questions.explain: Clues: the appositive defines blank (i): 'terrestrial microbes that had seeped in after it landed', that is, intruders from outside. Contaminants. Trap: relics (remnants of the past) is the defenders' interpretation, ancient remains, the opposite of later intrusion. Progenitors (ancestors) is unsupported. Blank (ii): 'forced to retreat to the more X claim that ... merely consistent with' needs a weaker claim: modest. Traps: sweeping and incontrovertible (impossible to dispute) are stronger, but one does not 'retreat' to a stronger claim, and 'merely' signals weakness. contaminants = substances that pollute or corrupt; progenitors = ancestors; incontrovertible = not open to question. Lesson: 'retreat' and 'merely' are direction signals; a retreat always moves to a weaker position.

questions.stem: Early reviewers dismissed the poet's fragmentary style as mere carelessness, and the label "unfinished" was applied to her work so often and so (i)_____ that by 1930 the term had become a (ii)_____ among critics, used less to describe her poems than to belittle them.
questions.explain: Clue: reviewers "dismissed" her style, and the term was used "less to describe her poems than to belittle them." Signal: "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) mockingly, (ii) insult word. Derisively fits the dismissive tone; pejorative is exactly a word used to belittle. Trap: misnomer means a WRONG name, but the sentence never says the label was inaccurate, only that it became an insult. Neologism fails because the term already existed. Words: derisively = with scorn; diffidently = shyly, without confidence; pejorative = expressing contempt; misnomer = an inaccurate name; neologism = a newly coined word. Lesson: in a consequence clause, match the exact result stated (belittle = pejorative), not a near-neighbor (inaccurate = misnomer).

questions.stem: Although the painter was celebrated in her lifetime as (i)_____, admirers praising how freely she broke with academic convention, recent archival work suggests that her innovations were far more (ii)_____ than this reputation implies: her notebooks show years of careful study of the very masters she was thought to have rejected.
questions.explain: Clue: (i) is glossed by "broke with academic convention"; (ii) is explained after the colon by "careful study of the very masters she was thought to have rejected." Signal: "Although" and "far more ... than this reputation implies" (contrast with the reputation). Predict: (i) rule-breaker, (ii) indebted to tradition. Iconoclast and derivative fit. Trap: radical repeats the reputation instead of contrasting with it; spontaneous clashes with "years of careful study." Epigone is the opposite-direction trap for (i). Words: iconoclast = one who attacks established conventions; epigone = an imitative follower; dilettante = a dabbler; derivative = drawn from earlier sources. Lesson: when the second half says "more X than the reputation implies," X must push AGAINST the reputation.

questions.stem: The composer's late quartets, long regarded as (i)_____ works accessible only to specialists, have lately found a surprisingly broad audience; what once seemed forbidding density now strikes many listeners as (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "accessible only to specialists" defines (i); "what once seemed forbidding density now strikes many" sets up a re-evaluation of the SAME density. Signal: "once ... now" (contrast in judgment, not in the music). Predict: (i) obscure, (ii) density seen positively. Recondite and absorbing complexity fit. Trap: superficial charm matches "broad audience" but contradicts "density"; the music did not get simpler, listeners changed. Arid formalism keeps the old negative view. Words: recondite = little known, abstruse; insipid = bland; ephemeral = short-lived; arid formalism = dry concern with form. Lesson: when a sentence says the same quality is now seen differently, keep the quality and flip only the evaluation.

questions.stem: Hume's critics accused him of a (i)_____ that would dissolve all knowledge, yet his own position was more modest. He doubted that causal inference could be rationally justified, not that it was indispensable; his skepticism was thus (ii)_____ rather than corrosive of ordinary belief.
questions.explain: Clue: "dissolve all knowledge" defines (i); "more modest" and "rather than corrosive" define (ii). Signal: "yet" and "rather than" (contrast). Predict: (i) total denial, (ii) limited. Nihilism fits the critics' charge; circumscribed means limited in scope. Trap: sweeping matches what the critics claimed, not what Hume held, so it contradicts "more modest." Credulity is the opposite of doubt; dogmatism asserts rather than dissolves. Words: nihilism = rejection of all knowledge or value; credulity = readiness to believe; dogmatism = rigid assertion; circumscribed = limited; inchoate = only partly formed. Lesson: separate the critics' view from the author's view; each blank belongs to one of them.

questions.stem: The central bank had overestimated growth for so many consecutive quarters that markets stopped treating its forecasts as neutral estimates; by the end of the decade, an official prediction of growth was read less as information than as (i)_____, and analysts routinely (ii)_____ it before incorporating it into their own models.
questions.explain: Clue: "overestimated growth" repeatedly and "stopped treating ... as neutral." Signal: "so ... that" (consequence) and "less as information than as." Predict: (i) optimistic bias, (ii) marked it down. Wishful thinking names an optimistic bias; discounted means reduced its weight. Trap: inflated reverses the correction; if forecasts run too high, you adjust them DOWN. Prudent understatement would fit a bank that underestimated. Disinterested analysis repeats the "neutral" reading the markets abandoned. Words: disinterested = impartial (not bored); discounted = regarded as less reliable, marked down; corroborated = confirmed. Lesson: trace the direction of the bias first, then choose the correction that runs opposite to it.

questions.stem: Madison regarded the multiplicity of factions not as a threat to be (i)_____ but as a safeguard: in a large republic, he argued, so many interests would compete that no single one could easily (ii)_____ the rest.
questions.explain: Clue: "threat" vs "safeguard"; "so many interests would compete." Signal: "not ... but" and "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) removed, (ii) dominate. Extirpated is what one does to a threat; subjugate is what competition prevents. Trap: cultivated and celebrated are what one does to a safeguard, so they belong to the wrong half of the "not ... but." Conciliate is the opposite of domination. Words: extirpate = root out completely; conciliate = placate, win over; emulate = imitate; subjugate = bring under control. Lesson: in "not as A to be (i) but as B," the blank must suit A, the rejected view.

questions.stem: Ethnographers once assumed that the tight-knit neighborhood they studied was (i)_____, its residents bound by shared origins and values. Closer observation revealed instead a community whose cohesion was (ii)_____: neighbors cooperated on practical matters while privately harboring deep disagreements.
questions.explain: Clue: (i) is glossed by "bound by shared origins and values"; (ii) by "cooperated on practical matters while privately harboring deep disagreements." Signal: "once assumed ... revealed instead" (contrast). Predict: (i) uniform, (ii) practical, not value-based. Homogeneous and functional fit. Trap: fractious describes what observers FOUND, not what they assumed, so it breaks the "once assumed" half. Organic and unanimous both imply shared values, contradicting "deep disagreements." Words: homogeneous = uniform in kind; fractious = quarrelsome; transient = temporary; functional = serving a practical purpose; organic = naturally unified. Lesson: when a sentence contrasts an assumption with a finding, check which half each blank sits in.

questions.stem: The novelist's prose is so (i)_____ that readers accustomed to her contemporaries' baroque sentences often mistake its plainness for poverty of imagination; only on rereading does one notice how much is (ii)_____ in what she declines to say.
questions.explain: Clue: "plainness," contrast with "baroque sentences," and "what she declines to say." Signal: "so ... that" and "only on rereading" (a hidden richness). Predict: (i) spare, (ii) suggested. Austere and implied fit. Trap: florid and turgid describe the contemporaries' baroque style, the opposite of plainness. Belabored contradicts "declines to say"; obscured is negative, while rereading reveals value. Words: austere = severely plain; florid = elaborately ornate; turgid = swollen, pompous; belabored = overworked. Lesson: if a blank is restated by a later noun ("plainness"), the answer must match that noun, not the foil it is contrasted with.

questions.stem: So many forgeries of the sculptor's work circulated in the decades after his death that collectors grew (i)_____ of any piece lacking documented provenance; as a result, several genuine works with gaps in their histories were (ii)_____ and sold for a fraction of their worth.
questions.explain: Clue: "so many forgeries" leads to an attitude toward undocumented pieces; "sold for a fraction of their worth" follows. Signal: "so ... that" and "as a result" (two consequences). Predict: (i) suspicious, (ii) doubted. Chary and impugned fit. Trap: credulous and heedless run opposite to caution. Vindicated and prized clash with "sold for a fraction of their worth." Words: chary = cautious, wary; credulous = too ready to believe; heedless = careless; impugned = called into question; vindicated = cleared of doubt. Lesson: chain the consequences: forgeries lead to suspicion, which leads to genuine works being doubted and undervalued.

questions.stem: The critic insisted that the conductor's tempos were (i)_____, yet even she conceded that his recordings, heard in sequence, revealed a (ii)_____ so consistent that it could only have been deliberate.
questions.explain: Clue: "so consistent that it could only have been deliberate." Signal: "yet even she conceded" means the concession goes AGAINST her claim. Predict: (i) arbitrary, (ii) underlying logic. Capricious and rationale fit. Trap: methodical in (i) agrees with "deliberate," so "yet ... conceded" would have nothing to concede; it fits locally but breaks the contrast. Stately and grandeur also agree with each other, again killing the contrast. Spontaneity contradicts "deliberate." Words: capricious = given to sudden, unpredictable change; methodical = orderly; stately = dignified, slow; rationale = underlying reason. Lesson: with "yet ... conceded," blank (i) must be something blank (ii) undercuts.

questions.stem: Far from being a (i)_____ thinker who arrived at his conclusions through sudden intuition, Spinoza proceeded with a rigor that some readers find almost (ii)_____: each proposition is derived from definitions and axioms laid down at the outset, in the manner of geometry.
questions.explain: Clue: (i) is glossed by "sudden intuition"; (ii) describes "a rigor" pushed to geometric extremes. Signal: "Far from" (contrast) and the colon (explanation). Predict: (i) unsystematic, (ii) excessively strict, wearying. Desultory and oppressive fit. Trap: meticulous describes what Spinoza WAS, so it breaks "far from." Cursory and capricious contradict "rigor." Words: desultory = lacking plan, jumping between things; meticulous = very careful; derivative = unoriginal; cursory = hasty; capricious = whimsical; oppressive = burdensome. Lesson: "Far from being X" means X is the opposite of the description that follows; do not pick the word that describes the subject.

questions.stem: The minister described the new tariff as a temporary measure to shelter infant industries. Twenty years later it remained in force, its original rationale long since (i)_____; the industries it protected had matured, yet the duty itself had proved (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "temporary measure" vs "Twenty years later it remained in force"; "industries ... had matured." Signal: "yet" (contrast between matured industries and the persistent duty). Predict: (i) outdated, (ii) hard to remove. Obsolete and entrenched fit. Trap: provisional repeats the minister's "temporary" claim that the sentence refutes. Compelling and reaffirmed contradict maturity: grown industries need no shelter. Salutary does not contrast with maturity, so it breaks "yet." Words: obsolete = no longer relevant; entrenched = firmly established, hard to dislodge; provisional = temporary; salutary = beneficial. Lesson: a no-signal stem still has logic; here time passing plus "remained in force" implies persistence.

questions.stem: The reform party's leaders compromised so often with the very interests they had promised to confront that their followers began to regard each new concession as (i)_____; by the next election, the word "reform" in the party's name struck most voters as (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "compromised so often with the very interests they had promised to confront." Signal: "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) a sellout, (ii) an inaccurate label. A betrayal and a misnomer fit: the party no longer reforms, so its name is wrong. Trap: a pejorative would require the word "reform" itself to become an insult; nothing says that. (This is the mirror of the "pejorative vs misnomer" error: here the name is inaccurate, not insulting.) An aberration contradicts "so often"; a masterstroke is the opposite judgment. Words: misnomer = a wrong or inaccurate name; pejorative = a word expressing contempt; aberration = a departure from the norm; mandate = authority granted by voters. Lesson: ask whether the label became FALSE (misnomer) or became an INSULT (pejorative).

questions.stem: Studies of upward mobility often (i)_____ the role of individual effort, crediting success to diligence alone; such accounts tend to obscure the (ii)_____ advantages, from family networks to inherited wealth, that make diligence pay off for some and not for others.
questions.explain: Clue: "crediting success to diligence alone" and "family networks to inherited wealth." Signal: semicolon (continuation: the second clause explains the cost of the first). Predict: (i) exaggerate, (ii) systemic. Overstate and structural fit. Trap: discount is the opposite direction; the studies give effort TOO MUCH weight. Document is too neutral for "alone." Meritocratic describes the effort story itself, not family networks; negligible contradicts "make diligence pay off." Words: discount = treat as unimportant; structural = arising from social arrangements; meritocratic = rewarding individual merit. Lesson: "alone" is a strong clue for overstatement; watch the direction.

questions.stem: Although the biographer cannot claim to be (i)_____ (whole decades of her subject's life survive in no record), she is (ii)_____ in using the fragments that do remain, coaxing from a laundry list or a misdated letter insights that more complete archives have not yielded to others.
questions.explain: Clue: the parenthesis explains (i): missing decades means she cannot be complete. "Coaxing ... insights" from scraps explains (ii). Signal: "Although" (concession). Predict: (i) thorough, (ii) clever with little. Exhaustive and resourceful fit. Trap: encyclopedic means comprehensive, which repeats what she "cannot claim"; it sounds like praise but contradicts blank (i). Cursory contradicts "coaxing." Perceptive in (i) clashes with (ii): she clearly IS perceptive. Words: exhaustive = complete; partisan = biased; resourceful = clever at using limited means; cursory = hasty; encyclopedic = comprehensive. Lesson: before choosing blank (ii), reread what blank (i) denied; never praise her for the very thing she lacks.

questions.stem: Critics who found the photographer's images (i)_____ missed the point: she deliberately chose the most banal subjects (parking lots, motel rooms, empty storefronts) precisely to show that the commonplace could be (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "most banal subjects" and "missed the point." Signal: colon (explanation) and "precisely to show." Predict: (i) dull, (ii) striking. Mundane captures the critics' complaint; arresting is what she aimed to show the commonplace could be. Trap: tedious agrees with the critics, so it destroys "missed the point." Sublime is what she wanted viewers to see, not the critics' complaint. Lurid means sensational, not banal. Words: mundane = ordinary, dull; sublime = awe-inspiring; lurid = shocking, sensational; arresting = striking, holding attention; transient = fleeting. Lesson: "missed the point" means the critics' word and the artist's goal must point in opposite directions.

questions.stem: The folk melodies the composer collected were never quoted verbatim in his symphonies. He absorbed their modal inflections and irregular rhythms so thoroughly that they became (i)_____ to his idiom, audible everywhere but locatable nowhere; scholars searching for direct borrowings have come away (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "absorbed ... so thoroughly," "audible everywhere but locatable nowhere," "never quoted verbatim." Signal: none explicit; "so ... that" plus the semicolon give consequence. Predict: (i) part of, (ii) with nothing. Intrinsic and empty-handed fit: absorbed melodies cannot be found as quotations. Trap: vindicated would mean the scholars found borrowings, contradicting "never quoted verbatim." Extraneous and antithetical are opposites of "absorbed." Words: intrinsic = belonging to the essential nature; extraneous = external, irrelevant; antithetical = directly opposed; vindicated = proved right. Lesson: when there is no signal word, the first sentence usually states the fact the blanks must respect.

questions.stem: To call the utilitarian's argument (i)_____ is not to call it false: its premises may each be plausible and its conclusion true, yet the inference from one to the other may still be (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: true premises and a true conclusion, "yet the inference ... may still be" flawed. Signal: "is not to call it" plus "yet" (a defect that is not falsity). Predict: (i) flawed in reasoning, (ii) faulty. Invalid and fallacious fit: an argument can reach a true conclusion by bad logic. Trap: cogent and rigorous are the opposite direction; persuasive is positive and breaks "yet." Novel has no link to the colon's explanation. Words: invalid = conclusion does not follow from premises; cogent = clear and convincing; fallacious = based on faulty reasoning. Lesson: the colon tells you what (i) means; pick the word the explanation defines.

questions.stem: Proponents of the policy predicted that cutting the tax would so stimulate investment that revenues would rise; in the event, investment barely (i)_____, and the resulting shortfall in revenue proved anything but (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: the prediction failed ("in the event") and there was a "shortfall." Signal: "barely" and "anything but" (a double reversal). Predict: (i) moved, (ii) small. Budged and negligible fit: investment hardly moved, and the shortfall was NOT small. Trap: severe and substantial describe the shortfall correctly, but "anything but" flips them, so they say the shortfall was small. Plummeted and surged do not pair with "barely." Words: budge = move slightly; plummet = fall sharply; negligible = too small to matter. Lesson: "anything but X" means "not X at all"; pick the word that is the OPPOSITE of what actually happened.

questions.stem: Hobbes's sovereign is often caricatured as a tyrant answerable to no one, but this reading (i)_____ the one limit Hobbes did impose: subjects retain the right to resist when their lives are threatened, since self-preservation was the very end for which they (ii)_____ their liberty.
questions.explain: Clue: "caricatured ... answerable to no one" vs "the one limit Hobbes did impose." Signal: "but" (contrast). Predict: (i) ignores, (ii) gave up. Neglects fits a caricature that omits a limit; surrendered fits the social contract, in which liberty is given up for safety. Trap: underscores is the opposite: a reading that stresses the limit could not call the sovereign answerable to no one. Exaggerates also implies the limit is acknowledged. Reclaimed is what resistance does, not the original bargain. Words: caricature = a distorting exaggeration; neglect = fail to attend to; underscore = emphasize. Lesson: a "caricature" leaves something out; the blank must name the omission.

questions.stem: The survey's questions were worded so (i)_____ that respondents could read almost any meaning into them; consequently, the apparent consensus the researchers reported was less a finding than (ii)_____ of their methods.
questions.explain: Clue: "read almost any meaning into them" and "apparent consensus." Signal: "so ... that" and "consequently" (consequence). Predict: (i) ambiguously, (ii) product, side effect. Equivocally and an artifact fit: the agreement was created by the vague wording, not discovered. Trap: a confirmation treats the consensus as real, contradicting "apparent" and "less a finding." Pointedly is the opposite of ambiguous; tersely means briefly, which does not cause ambiguity. Words: equivocal = open to more than one interpretation; artifact = a result produced by the method rather than the thing studied. Lesson: "apparent" plus "less a finding than" signals that the result is an illusion created by the method.

questions.stem: The poet's admirers praise her (i)_____, but her detractors are not wrong that her refusal to waste a syllable sometimes yields lines so compressed as to be (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "refusal to waste a syllable" and "so compressed." Signal: "but ... not wrong" (a fair criticism of the same trait). Predict: (i) brevity, (ii) obscure. Concision and cryptic fit: too much compression makes lines hard to decode. Trap: prolixity is the opposite-direction word (wordiness), and diffuse is likewise the opposite of compressed. Candor is a virtue unrelated to syllables; mawkish is about sentiment, not compression. Words: concision = brevity of expression; prolixity = tedious wordiness; cryptic = mysterious, hard to understand; diffuse = spread out, wordy; mawkish = excessively sentimental. Lesson: a virtue pushed too far becomes its own vice; keep both blanks on the same axis (compression).

questions.stem: The restorers removed centuries of darkened varnish from the fresco. Viewers who had long admired its somber, brooding palette were dismayed to find colors of an almost (i)_____ brightness. The gloom they had taken as the painter's intention was, it turned out, (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "darkened varnish" removed; viewers "dismayed"; gloom they "had taken as the painter's intention." Signal: none explicit; "it turned out" signals a reversal. Predict: (i) loud, overly bright, (ii) caused by age. Garish fits both "brightness" and dismay; an accretion of time names the varnish. Trap: a deliberate effect restates the mistaken belief that "it turned out" corrects. Muted and funereal describe the old, dark appearance. Words: garish = obtrusively bright; muted = subdued; funereal = gloomy; accretion = gradual buildup. Lesson: "it turned out" means the blank must overturn what people had assumed.

questions.stem: Although the tenor's voice was not large, his (i)_____ phrasing allowed him to dominate halls that defeated louder singers; he understood that audibility depends less on sheer volume than on (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "voice was not large" yet he dominated halls; "less on sheer volume than on." Signal: "Although" and "less ... than" (contrast). Predict: (i) sharp, precise, (ii) precision. Incisive and clarity of articulation fit. Trap: force of lungs is just "sheer volume" again, which the sentence ranks lower. Bombastic implies loudness and pomp, clashing with "not large"; slack could not dominate a hall. Breadth of repertoire has nothing to do with audibility. Words: incisive = sharp, clear, penetrating; slack = loose, lacking vigor; bombastic = high-sounding, inflated. Lesson: "less on A than on B" means B must differ from A; reject options that restate A.

questions.stem: Kant's prose is notoriously (i)_____, yet those who persist through its thickets often find that the difficulty is not gratuitous; the convolutions mirror genuine (ii)_____ in the problems he was trying to solve.
questions.explain: Clue: "thickets," "difficulty," "convolutions." Signal: "yet" turns from complaint to defense; "not gratuitous" means the difficulty is justified. Predict: (i) hard to read, (ii) complexity. Impenetrable and intricacies fit. Trap: limpid is the opposite-direction word (clear). Glib means superficially fluent, not difficult. Banalities would make the difficulty pointless, contradicting "not gratuitous"; resolutions are solutions, but convolutions mirror problems, not answers. Words: impenetrable = impossible to understand; limpid = clear; glib = fluent but shallow; gratuitous = uncalled for. Lesson: "not gratuitous" means "justified"; the blank must supply the justification.

questions.stem: Because the commodity's price had swung wildly for a decade, the government's promise to (i)_____ it was greeted with skepticism; few believed that a buffer stock so (ii)_____ could absorb shocks of that magnitude.
