questions.explain: Clue: "swung wildly" and "absorb shocks." Signal: "Because" (cause) and "skepticism ... few believed" (doubt). Predict: (i) steady, (ii) small. Stabilize fits a promise aimed at wild swings; meager explains the doubt. Trap: ample would make the stock adequate and undercut "skepticism." Volatile describes the price, not the size of a reserve. Liberalize and inflate do not answer wild swings. Words: stabilize = make steady; liberalize = remove controls; meager = inadequate in amount; ample = more than enough; volatile = liable to sudden change. Lesson: "skepticism" and "few believed" call for a word that makes the plan look inadequate.

questions.stem: The ambassador's reputation for (i)_____ was well earned: in thirty years of negotiation she never once made a promise she could not keep or a threat she did not mean, a record that made her counterparts (ii)_____ to call her bluffs.
questions.explain: Clue: "never once made a promise she could not keep or a threat she did not mean." Signal: colon (explanation) and "a record that made" (consequence). Predict: (i) honesty, (ii) unwilling. Probity and loath fit: if her threats are always real, calling a "bluff" is dangerous. Trap: duplicity is the opposite-direction word (deceit); bluster suggests empty threats. Eager reverses the consequence. Words: probity = strict honesty, integrity; duplicity = deceitfulness; bluster = loud empty talk; loath = reluctant. Lesson: work out the consequence step by step: real threats mean no one dares to test them.

questions.stem: Much early scholarship treated the city's immigrant enclaves as way stations whose residents would soon (i)_____ into the wider society; yet many enclaves persisted for generations, suggesting that they served less as transit points than as (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "way stations," "persisted for generations," "less as transit points than as." Signal: "yet" (contrast). Predict: (i) blend in, (ii) lasting homes. Assimilate and enduring communities fit. Trap: temporary refuges and points of departure both restate "way stations" and "transit points," the view the sentence rejects. Withdraw and secede move away from the wider society, the wrong direction for a way station. Words: enclave = a distinct group within a larger territory; assimilate = become absorbed into a culture; secede = formally withdraw. Lesson: "less as X than as" means the answer must contrast with X; reject options that are X in other words.

questions.stem: The critic's early reviews were so uniformly (i)_____ that publishers came to dread them; later, when he began to praise a few writers, the very rarity of his approval made it (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "publishers came to dread them"; "rarity of his approval." Signal: "so ... that" (consequence) and "later" (contrast in time). Predict: (i) harsh, (ii) highly valued. Scathing and coveted fit: what is rare is prized. Trap: laudatory is the opposite direction; no one dreads praise. Equivocal reviews would not inspire dread. Worthless and predictable reverse the logic of rarity. Words: scathing = severely critical; laudatory = praising; equivocal = ambiguous; coveted = eagerly desired. Lesson: scarcity creates value; "very rarity ... made it" points to something prized.

questions.stem: The museum's new wing, intended to (i)_____ the original building's neoclassical facade, instead overwhelms it; its glass bulk makes the older structure look less like a centerpiece than like (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "intended to ... instead overwhelms it." Signal: "instead" means the intention differs from the result. Predict: (i) enhance, set off, (ii) something minor. Complement and an afterthought fit. Trap: eclipse describes what the wing actually did, so it cannot be the intention; it fits locally but breaks "instead." Replicate fails because glass does not copy neoclassical stone. A culmination and a model are prominent, contradicting "less like a centerpiece." Words: complement = complete, enhance by contrast; eclipse = overshadow; replicate = copy; culmination = highest point. Lesson: "intended ... instead" sets intention against result; the blank sits on the intention side.

questions.stem: Jazz improvisation is sometimes imagined as pure invention, conjured from nothing in the moment. Musicians themselves describe something closer to (i)_____: years of absorbing licks, patterns, and harmonic formulas that, in performance, are recombined so fluidly that the result sounds (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "conjured from nothing" (the myth) vs "years of absorbing ... formulas" (the reality); "recombined so fluidly." Signal: "something closer to" (correction) and "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) memory, (ii) spontaneous. Recollection and extemporaneous fit: stored material is recalled yet sounds improvised. Trap: rehearsed fits "years of absorbing" locally but contradicts "so fluidly"; fluency makes it sound unplanned. Inspiration and revelation restate the "from nothing" myth. Derivative ignores "fluidly." Words: extemporaneous = done without preparation; derivative = unoriginal. Lesson: in "so ... that," the result follows from the specific cause (fluid recombination), not from the general context.

questions.stem: The philosopher hedged every claim with so many qualifications that his critics could find nothing to refute; the price of this (i)_____, however, was that his admirers could find nothing to (ii)_____ either.
questions.explain: Clue: "hedged every claim with so many qualifications"; "nothing to refute" ... "nothing to ___ either." Signal: "the price of this ... however" (a cost) and "either" (parallel). Predict: (i) carefulness, (ii) adopt. Caution and embrace fit: critics have nothing to attack, admirers nothing to hold on to. Trap: dispute repeats "refute," but admirers do not dispute; the parallel needs the admirers' own action. Audacity is the opposite of hedging; clarity is undermined by endless qualification. Words: hedge = qualify to avoid commitment; audacity = boldness; refute = disprove. Lesson: "either" sets up a parallel; match each group with its own natural action.

questions.stem: Economists had long assumed that consumers were (i)_____ calculators who weighed every purchase against its alternatives; experiments showing that the mere order in which options are presented sways choices have made that assumption look (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "weighed every purchase against its alternatives" vs "mere order ... sways choices." Signal: none explicit; "had long assumed" plus contrary evidence implies the assumption is outdated. Predict: (i) logical, (ii) outdated. Rational and quaint fit. Trap: prescient and robust treat the assumption as confirmed, the opposite of what the experiments show. Impulsive and myopic describe the experiments' consumers, not the calculators of the old assumption. Words: myopic = short-sighted; quaint = charmingly old-fashioned, outdated; prescient = foreseeing the future; robust = strong, holding up. Lesson: "had long assumed" usually sets up an assumption about to be undermined.

questions.stem: The constitution's framers left the scope of executive power deliberately (i)_____, trusting that future generations would settle by practice what they could not settle by text; the result has been two centuries of (ii)_____ over precisely those questions.
questions.explain: Clue: "settle by practice what they could not settle by text." Signal: "the result has been" (consequence). Predict: (i) unclear, (ii) dispute. Ambiguous and contention fit: what text leaves open, later generations fight over. Trap: explicit and circumscribed both mean settled by text, the opposite of what the framers did. Consensus contradicts the idea that the questions still had to be settled; indifference contradicts "precisely those questions" being pressing. Words: circumscribed = clearly limited; contention = heated disagreement. Lesson: in a consequence clause, ask what follows from the specific gap the first clause created.

questions.stem: Contrary to the stereotype of the (i)_____ teenager who communicates in monosyllables, the adolescents in the study proved (ii)_____ when asked about subjects that mattered to them, often talking for an hour without prompting.
questions.explain: Clue: "communicates in monosyllables" defines (i); "talking for an hour without prompting" defines (ii). Signal: "Contrary to" (contrast). Predict: (i) silent, (ii) talkative. Taciturn and voluble fit. Trap: garrulous is the opposite-direction pick for (i); it describes the study's teens, not the stereotype. Laconic and reticent are synonyms of taciturn, so they belong to the stereotype, not the finding. Words: taciturn = habitually silent; garrulous = excessively talkative; precocious = advanced for one's age; voluble = speaking fluently and at length; laconic = using few words; reticent = reserved. Lesson: when you know a word pair (taciturn / garrulous), locate each blank's own clue before choosing.

questions.stem: Readers who know the novel only through its film adaptation imagine a (i)_____ romance; the book itself is far darker, its love story merely the pretext for a (ii)_____ dissection of the class system that made such love impossible.
questions.explain: Clue: "the book itself is far darker" (so the film version is light); "dissection of the class system." Signal: semicolon with "far darker" (contrast between film and book). Predict: (i) sweet, (ii) unsparing. Sentimental and merciless fit. Trap: bleak describes the book, not the film, so it breaks the contrast. Satirical is not the opposite of "darker." Genial and cursory contradict "far darker" and "dissection." Words: sentimental = appealing to tender emotions; satirical = mocking; merciless = showing no pity; genial = friendly; cursory = hasty. Lesson: "far darker" tells you the first blank must be light; do not fill it with the book's own quality.

questions.stem: Because the medieval workshop prized fidelity to established models over personal expression, its artists rarely signed their works; so thoroughly was individual style (i)_____ that modern scholars can often assign a panel to a workshop but almost never to (ii)_____ hand.
questions.explain: Clue: "prized fidelity to established models over personal expression"; "rarely signed." Signal: "Because" and "so ... that" (cause and consequence). Predict: (i) suppressed, (ii) individual. Subordinated and particular fit: scholars can name the workshop but not the individual. Trap: anonymous and collective describe what scholars CAN identify (the group), but the sentence contrasts the workshop with a single hand. Celebrated and cultivated are the opposite direction. Words: subordinate = treat as less important; cultivate = develop; particular = specific, individual. Lesson: "assign to X but never to Y" means Y contrasts with X; here workshop vs individual.

questions.stem: The symphony's premiere was a fiasco, the audience jeering through its dissonant final movement; yet within a generation the work had become so (i)_____ a part of the repertoire that its (ii)_____ is now hard to imagine.
questions.explain: Clue: "fiasco," "jeering" vs "within a generation ... part of the repertoire." Signal: "yet" (contrast) and "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) established, (ii) its bad start. Ingrained and early notoriety fit: the work is now so established that its scandalous premiere is hard to picture. Trap: canonical status is the work's present condition, which is easy to imagine, since it is true. Peripheral and precarious contradict becoming a fixture. Technical difficulty is never mentioned. Words: ingrained = firmly fixed, deep-rooted; peripheral = marginal; precarious = unstable; notoriety = fame for something bad; canonical = accepted as a classic. Lesson: "so established that its ___ is hard to imagine" points backward to the past it has outgrown.

questions.stem: Socrates professed (i)_____, insisting that he knew nothing; but his interlocutors often suspected that the profession was (ii)_____, a pose that allowed him to expose their ignorance while concealing his own convictions.
questions.explain: Clue: "insisting that he knew nothing" defines (i); "a pose" and "concealing his own convictions" define (ii). Signal: "but ... suspected" (contrast). Predict: (i) not knowing, (ii) insincere. Ignorance and disingenuous fit. Trap: heartfelt is the opposite direction; "a pose" is not sincere. Incoherent attacks the logic, not the sincerity. Omniscience is the opposite of "knew nothing." Words: profess = claim openly; omniscience = knowing everything; disingenuous = not candid, pretending to know less than one does; incoherent = lacking logical connection. Lesson: an appositive ("a pose that ...") right after a blank is its definition; read it before the choices.

questions.stem: The firm's quarterly report was a masterpiece of (i)_____. Losses appeared as "negative growth," layoffs as "workforce optimization," and a failed product launch as "a learning opportunity." Investors who read past the vocabulary found the company's position (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: losses, layoffs, and failure renamed with soft phrases; investors who "read past the vocabulary." Signal: none explicit; the examples define (i), and "read past" implies a reality different from the wording. Predict: (i) soft-pedaling, (ii) dangerous. Euphemism and parlous fit. Trap: robust accepts the report's spin. Ambiguous fails because the facts beneath (losses, layoffs) are plainly bad. Candor is the opposite-direction word; hyperbole is exaggeration, but these phrases understate. Words: euphemism = a mild term for something unpleasant; candor = frankness; hyperbole = exaggeration; parlous = precarious, dangerous. Lesson: examples are definitions; a list of soft labels defines euphemism, not hyperbole.

questions.stem: The "temporary" emergency powers granted during the war were renewed so routinely in the decades that followed that the adjective eventually became (i)_____; scholars now cite the case as a textbook example of how exceptional measures can become (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "temporary" in quotation marks; "renewed so routinely in the decades." Signal: "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) no longer accurate, used with irony, (ii) routine. Ironic and normalized fit. Trap: derogatory would mean "temporary" became an insult; it merely stopped being true. Apt is the opposite: decades of renewal make "temporary" inaccurate. Abolished contradicts renewal; exceptional repeats the starting point instead of the change. Words: ironic = meaning the opposite of what is said; apt = fitting; derogatory = disparaging; normalized = made routine. Lesson: a label that stops matching reality becomes ironic (or a misnomer), not an insult.

questions.stem: The sociologist's findings on neighborhood trust were initially greeted as (i)_____, overturning decades of received wisdom; but when other research teams repeatedly failed to reproduce them, enthusiasm gave way to (ii)_____.
questions.explain: Clue: "overturning decades of received wisdom"; "failed to reproduce"; "enthusiasm gave way to." Signal: "initially" and "but" (change over time). Predict: (i) groundbreaking, (ii) doubt. Revolutionary and skepticism fit. Trap: spurious fits the LATER verdict, not the initial greeting, so it breaks "initially greeted" and "enthusiasm." Pedestrian contradicts "overturning." Adulation continues the enthusiasm rather than replacing it; complacency does not follow failed replication. Words: pedestrian = dull, ordinary; spurious = false, fake; adulation = excessive praise. Lesson: time markers (initially / later) assign each blank to a moment; fill each with that moment's attitude.

questions.stem: The memoirist is too (i)_____ to flatter herself: where another writer might have cast her younger self as a misunderstood rebel, she presents a girl who was vain, (ii)_____, and frequently cruel, sparing herself none of the judgments she passes on others.
questions.explain: Clue: "too ___ to flatter herself" and "sparing herself none of the judgments." Signal: "too ... to" and a list "vain, ___, and frequently cruel" (continuation of faults). Predict: (i) honest, unsentimental, (ii) a fault. Clear-eyed and petty fit. Trap: vainglorious and indulgent would make her LIKELY to flatter herself, reversing "too ... to." Magnanimous and long-suffering are virtues that break a list of faults. Words: clear-eyed = realistic, unsentimental; vainglorious = boastfully vain; petty = small-minded; magnanimous = generous, forgiving. Lesson: a list in a series takes items of the same polarity; one virtue in a list of faults is a trap.

questions.stem: The forger's skill lay not in (i)_____ any single painting, which would have invited direct comparison, but in producing new works so (ii)_____ of the master's manner that experts assumed they were lost originals.
questions.explain: Clue: "which would have invited direct comparison" and "new works"; "experts assumed they were lost originals." Signal: "not in ... but in" (contrast between two methods). Predict: (i) duplicating, (ii) suggestive of. Copying and redolent fit. Trap: independent sounds like praise for "new works," but works independent of the master's manner would never pass as his. Dismissive does not take "of the master's manner" sensibly. Authenticating is the experts' job, not the forger's. Words: disparage = belittle; redolent of = strongly suggestive of; independent = not influenced by. Lesson: test the consequence: only a word meaning "like the master" leads experts to assume lost originals.

questions.stem: Critics who dismissed the minimalist composers as (i)_____, merely repeating a figure until the listener grew numb, overlooked the subtle (ii)_____ embedded in the repetition: each cycle differs from its predecessor by a single note or beat.
questions.explain: Clue: "merely repeating a figure until the listener grew numb" defines (i); "each cycle differs from its predecessor" defines (ii). Signal: "overlooked" (the critics missed something) and colon (explanation). Predict: (i) repetitive, (ii) change. Monotonous and variation fit. Trap: uniformity and stasis repeat the critics' charge, which "overlooked" says is wrong. Eclectic (drawing on many sources) and bombastic (inflated) do not match "merely repeating." Words: monotonous = tediously unvarying; eclectic = drawing from diverse sources; bombastic = pompous; stasis = inactivity, no change. Lesson: after "overlooked," the blank names what the critics missed, so it contradicts their view.

questions.stem: Pascal's wager does not attempt to prove that God exists. It argues instead that belief is the prudent bet given our uncertainty. Its force, then, is (i)_____ rather than evidential, and objections that it fails to supply (ii)_____ for God's existence miss its aim.
questions.explain: Clue: "does not attempt to prove" and "the prudent bet given our uncertainty." Signal: "then" (conclusion) and "rather than evidential" (contrast). Predict: (i) practical, (ii) evidence. Pragmatic and proof fit: the wager is about what is wise to do, so objecting that it lacks proof misses its aim. Trap: incentive is exactly what the wager DOES supply, so objecting that it lacks one would not miss its aim. Empirical is a kind of evidential reasoning, so it cannot contrast with "evidential." Theological names the topic, not the type of force. Words: pragmatic = concerned with practical consequences; empirical = based on observation. Lesson: "X rather than Y" requires X to be a genuine alternative to Y, not a version of it.

questions.stem: Critics of the merger warned that the combined firm would wield (i)_____ power, free to raise prices without fear of losing customers; regulators, however, found the market still so (ii)_____ that any attempt to do so would simply send buyers to rival suppliers.
questions.explain: Clue: "free to raise prices without fear of losing customers" defines (i); "send buyers to rival suppliers" defines (ii). Signal: "however" (contrast) and "so ... that" (consequence). Predict: (i) dominant over the market, (ii) full of rivals. Monopolistic and competitive fit. Trap: concentrated supports the critics' worry, the opposite of what "however" requires. Stagnant does not explain why buyers can switch. Negligible contradicts "free to raise prices"; fiduciary refers to trust duties, not market power. Words: monopolistic = controlling a market alone; fiduciary = involving a duty held in trust; concentrated (market) = dominated by few firms. Lesson: "however" flips the critics' claim; pick the market condition that defeats it.

questions.stem: The revolutionary leader's speeches were (i)_____, promising a complete break with the past; his conduct in office was strikingly (ii)_____, retaining most of the old regime's ministries, laws, and officials.
questions.explain: Clue: "promising a complete break with the past" defines (i); "retaining most of the old regime's ministries, laws, and officials" defines (ii). Signal: none explicit; "strikingly" and the content imply a contrast between words and deeds. Predict: (i) fiery, (ii) cautious, preserving. Incendiary and conservative fit. Trap: radical matches the speeches, not the conduct, and contradicts "retaining." Erratic implies inconsistency, but his conduct consistently preserved the old order. Conciliatory and tepid are the opposite of "complete break." Words: incendiary = inflammatory; conciliatory = intended to placate; tepid = lukewarm; conservative = favoring the existing order. Lesson: when no signal word appears, compare the two definitions; opposed content means opposed words.

questions.stem: Once a marker of genuine distinction, the honorary degree was conferred so indiscriminately (on donors, celebrities, and local officials alike) that it lost its (i)_____; by the century's end, recipients who listed it on their résumés risked appearing (ii)_____ rather than distinguished.
questions.explain: Clue: "marker of genuine distinction" and "conferred so indiscriminately." Signal: "so ... that" (consequence) and "rather than distinguished" (contrast). Predict: (i) prestige, (ii) showing off. Cachet and pretentious fit: flaunting a cheapened honor looks like pretending. Trap: eminent means distinguished, which the sentence rules out. Modest contradicts listing it on a résumé. Ubiquity and triviality are what the degree GAINED, not what it lost. Words: cachet = prestige; ubiquity = being everywhere; pretentious = claiming more importance than is warranted; eminent = famous, respected. Lesson: "lost its ___" needs a quality it had before; check which state the blank belongs to.

questions.stem: The scholar's edition is (i)_____ in its textual apparatus, recording every variant reading across a dozen manuscripts, yet (ii)_____ in its interpretive notes, which seldom venture beyond a line or two.
questions.explain: Clue: "recording every variant reading" defines (i); "seldom venture beyond a line or two" defines (ii). Signal: "yet" (contrast between the two parts). Predict: (i) complete, (ii) brief, economical. Painstaking and sparing fit. Trap: prolix is the opposite-direction word for (ii), meaning wordy; it would match blank (i)'s abundance, not the brevity described. Sketchy contradicts "every variant." Tendentious and dogmatic concern bias, not quantity. Words: painstaking = extremely thorough; textual apparatus = the record of variants in a scholarly edition; tendentious = promoting a particular view; sparing = economical, restrained; prolix = tediously long. Lesson: when each blank has its own definition, solve each against its own clue, then check that "yet" contrasts them.
